title: Kanaganahalli Shows a King's Face
subtitle: How A Buried Stupa Redrew the Faces of the Satavahanas
era: Kanaganahalli stupa phases, c. 1st century BCE-2nd century CE
moral: A single label in stone can reorder centuries.

sources.citation: ASI Karnataka Circle excavations at Kanaganahalli/Sannati, 1994-2001
sources.note: Recent excavation context for the mahastupa and portrait slabs.

sources.citation: Ajay Mitra Shastri, Kanaganahalli Inscriptions, Indian Historical Review Vol. 29 (2002/03)
sources.note: Primary scholarly publication of the Satavahana portrait inscriptions.

sources.citation: Akira Shimada, Early Buddhist Architecture in Context (2012); Andrew Ollett, Language of the Snakes (2017)
sources.note: Recent use of Kanaganahalli in Satavahana chronology and Buddhist art history.

panels.shot: dramatic three-quarter view of a weathered limestone slab with a royal figure, half-emerging from soil in golden excavation light

dialogue.text: For two thousand years the Satavahanas were names in books; at Kanaganahalli, a buried stupa raised their faces from stone and shook the very timeline of an empire.

panels.shot: wide aerial shot over the dry plains of northern Karnataka, the Krishna river curving past low mounds

dialogue.text: On the banks of the Krishna in northern Karnataka, villagers long circled a nameless mound, lighting lamps to a small shrine, never guessing they walked atop a forgotten mahastupa.

panels.shot: medium shot of archaeologists and workers opening a trench on the mound in the mid-1990s

dialogue.text: In 1994, the Archaeological Survey of India cut cautious trenches into the mound; brick by brick, the circle of a great stupa appeared, its broken limestone railings lying where they had fallen.

panels.shot: close-up of hands lifting a carved limestone slab from the trench edge

dialogue.text: Among the rubble, curved slabs of pale limestone emerged, carved with processions, stupas, elephants, and men with high turbans—railings that once wrapped the great dome in stories.

panels.shot: extreme close-up of a chiselled Brahmi label above a royal figure on a slab

dialogue.text: Then, on one slab, the stone spoke in letters: a crisp Prakrit label in early Brahmi script, carved above a seated figure like a caption anchoring image to name.

panels.shot: medium shot of Shilpi and an epigraphist squatting by the slab, intensely focused

dialogue.speaker: the_kanaganahalli_sculptors
dialogue.text: These letters… they fix a face to a king.

panels.shot: insert close-up of a scholar’s hand on paper, tracing the inscription while an imagined reconstruction floats above

dialogue.text: The label called him Rāja Siri Chimuko Sādavahano—Chimuka Satavahana—one of the earliest Satavahana rulers, now no longer an invisible name in texts but a carved presence before our eyes.

panels.shot: historic-style wide shot imagining the original railing in place around a gleaming stupa

dialogue.text: When the stupa was young, Chimuka’s portrait looked out over the circumambulation path, placed among Jataka tales and donors, proclaiming that the Satavahana house now sheltered the Buddha’s relics.

panels.shot: close-up on the portrait figure itself: a king in profile with ornaments and courtly posture

dialogue.text: The king is not idealized as a god; he is a man of flesh and cloth, with sober face, ornaments, and attendants, his royal body drawn into the same visual world as the devotees around him.

panels.shot: dramatic low-angle shot of Shilpi imagining the ancient sculptor at work on the same slab

dialogue.text: Some anonymous sculptor here, two millennia ago, made a daring choice: he placed a living king inside a Buddhist monument, giving the Satavahanas not just power over land but a place in sacred stone.

panels.shot: busy interior of an ancient workshop, with Shilpi’s past-self among fellow artisans planning panels

dialogue.speaker: the_kanaganahalli_sculptors
dialogue.text: We carve kings among stories, so future eyes will read patron and path together.

panels.shot: montage wide shot of multiple portrait slabs laid out in the excavation storehouse

dialogue.text: Kanaganahalli yielded more than one face: portraits of Satavahana kings, queens, and courts, each with labels, turning what had once been an almost faceless dynasty into a sequence of stone visages.

panels.shot: close-up of another inscription mentioning Year 16, with a scholar’s pencil circling the number

dialogue.text: One record spoke of a ‘Year 16’ in connection with the Satavahana line; scholars cautiously tied this to Simuka, the dynasty’s founder, giving his reign a relative anchor instead of pure Puranic guesswork.

panels.shot: split screen: on one side Puranic lists on palm leaves, on the other excavation plans and stratigraphy charts

dialogue.text: For centuries, the Satavahana chronology leaned on Puranic lists, full of gaps and contradictions; Kanaganahalli’s layers and labels forced those ghostly sequences to confront bricks, mortar, and dated stone.

panels.shot: medium shot of a modern historian at a desk comparing dates and maps of the Deccan

dialogue.text: Akira Shimada and others wove Kanaganahalli into a wider tapestry of early Buddhist sites, numismatics and paleography, using its stupa phases to narrow when the Satavahanas rose across the Deccan plateau.

panels.shot: dramatic mid-shot of another scholar with magnified Brahmi letters on a computer screen

dialogue.text: Yet the stone did not shout exact years; its script styles and archaeological phases only suggested a rough horizon, around the late first century BCE, leaving room for debate rather than final answers.

panels.shot: evocative shot of the stupa ruins at dusk with the river glinting beyond

dialogue.text: The stupa itself lies broken, its railing scattered, but its measured ruin now pins Satavahana power to a landscape of rivers, trade routes, and monasteries instead of floating in legendary time.

panels.shot: medium shot of Shilpi gently touching the portrait slab now in a site shelter

dialogue.speaker: the_kanaganahalli_sculptors
dialogue.text: We carved for the merit of donors; we did not know we carved for historians.

panels.shot: final wide shot blending past and present: villagers, archaeologists and the imagined ancient processions around the same stupa circle

dialogue.text: At Kanaganahalli, a single label chiselled above a king binds text to earth, legend to layer, reminding us that sometimes one careful word in stone can reorder centuries of history around it.
